newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin takes over as France's prime minister.
newsitem.headline: Jospin takes over as France's prime minister.

text.p: Socialist Lionel Jospin formally took office as France's prime minister on Tuesday and the party's European affairs spokeswoman pledged to stick to the timetable for a single European currency.

A relaxed Jospin shook hands with his defeated Gaullist predecessor Alain Juppe, who wore a fixed smile, at a brief ceremony in the courtyard of the prime minister's office. The two men met privately for just 13 minutes.

The 59-year-old Jospin, who plans to form a government by the end of the week, is likely to make his debut on the world stage on Thursday at a conference of the Socialist International in Malmo in Sweden, aides said.

Hours before he was appointed, Socialist Elisabeth Guigou, who may take the European affairs portfolio, sought to soothe financial markets worried about prospects for the euro currency following Sunday's leftist win in a parliamentary election.
Asked whether the new government would seek to ensure the euro is created by the target date of January 1, 1999, Guigou told RTL radio: "Of couse we must respect this deadline."
She added that the Maastricht Treaty on criteria for economic and monetary union must be completed with a separate chapter on employment.

"The treaty must be completed on certain points. Institutions must be reformed to enable Europe to decide and to be more democratic...In the name of the European left, I suggested at the intergovernmental conference (IGC) that there be a chapter on jobs," she said.
The IGC, aimed at reforming and streamling the European Union as it prepares to take on new members, is to culminate in the signing of a treaty in Amsterdam in two weeks time.

Earlier, Jospin met Communist leader Robert Hue to discuss the makeup of the government. The Socialists need help from leftist allies including the Communists and ecologists to gain an outright majority in parliament.

The Communists said on Monday they wanted to participate but sought undertakings from the Socialists to raise the national minimum wage by eight percent, take first steps to cut the work week to 35 hours from 39, cut value-added tax and ensure there would be no further austerity to qualify for the euro.
But an aide to Jospin said he had told Hue he wanted "a yes or no answer without conditions" on whether the Communists would come on board.
Without waiting for the formal handover, the leader of the country's second biggest trade union fired a warning shot across the bows of the as-yet-unformed government.

Louis Viannet, head of the Communist CGT, urged the new premier to swifly raise the national minimum wage and announce an end to privatisation, even before he convenes a planned conference on a cut in working hours and other issues.

"The government must say quickly what it plans to do about the minimum wage. After that, a whole series of issues will have to be negotiated, and will require very vigorous action by workers," Viannet told France-Inter radio.

"What I want to say to wage-earners is this: 'Don't wait for things to come down from above. Start from today, go and see the bosses and make your demands on working conditions and working hours," Viannet said.
Jospin was appointed on Monday by centre-right President Jacques Chirac, who had gambled disastrously by calling elections 10 months early.

Chirac had hoped for a new centre-right government to support him through the remainder of his seven-year term until 2002. But he misjudged the mood of the public, angry at his broken campaign promises to curb unemployment and slash taxes, and at government austerity policies to qualify for the euro.

Jospin has served notice he will not consider implementing further austerity measures before the introduction of the single currency. He has argued for a more flexible interpretation of the economic targets for joining it.
Socialist party spokesman Francois Hollande said on Monday that there could be no immediate broad action on salaries or taxes, though some symbolic measures would be taken by July.
He said it would not be realistic to set specific wage scales before a cabinet was formed.
